title: Boundary Value Problems by Finite Differences
short: Replace y″ by (yᵢ₊₁ − 2yᵢ + yᵢ₋₁)/h² at each inside grid point to get a tridiagonal linear system.
trouble: Students treat the known boundary values as unknowns, or forget to move them to the right-hand side.

blocks.html: A boundary value problem fixes $y$ at both ends of an interval instead of giving $y$ and $y'$ at the start, so stepping forward from one end does not work directly. Instead, put a grid on the interval, replace $y''$ by the second difference, and solve for all the unknown grid values at once with a linear system, using Solving with PA = LU.

For $y'' = f(x)$ on $[a, b]$ with $y(a) = \alpha$, $y(b) = \beta$, take $x_i = a + ih$, $i = 0, \ldots, N$, with $h = \frac{b - a}{N}$. The unknowns are $y_1, \ldots, y_{N-1}$; $y_0 = \alpha$ and $y_N = \beta$ are known. At each inside point, $$y_{i-1} - 2y_i + y_{i+1} = h^{2}f(x_i).$$

The equations form a tridiagonal system: $1, -2, 1$ around the diagonal. In the first and last equations the known boundary values move to the right-hand side. The error at the grid points is $O(h^{2})$, and the system is solved in $O(N)$ operations.

The second difference has truncation error $\frac{h^{2}}{12}y^{(4)}$, so the discrete equations differ from the true ones by $O(h^{2})$; for this kind of problem that carries over to the computed values. Each equation involves only three neighbors, so the matrix is tridiagonal. It is also symmetric and diagonally dominant (weakly), so elimination needs no pivoting and costs about $8N$ operations instead of $\frac{2}{3}N^{3}$.

blocks.title: A problem the method solves exactly
steps: Solve: $y_1 = \frac{1}{27}$, $y_2 = \frac{8}{27}$. The exact solution is $x^{3}$, and these are exact, because the second difference has no error for cubics.

blocks.title: A term in y
steps: System: $\begin{bmatrix} -2.25 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2.25 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2.25 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \\ y_3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}$ (the $y_4 = 1$ moved to the right).
Solution: $(0.1451, 0.3265, 0.5896)$. Exact: $\frac{\sinh 2x}{\sinh 2}$ gives $(0.1437, 0.3240, 0.5871)$: errors about $0.002$, and halving $h$ would cut them by about 4.

blocks.name: num-system

opts.task: Double the number of intervals and watch the error drop by about 4. Then tick the box that leaves the boundary values out.

blocks.cap: The finite-difference solution of y″ − 4y = 0, y(0) = 0, y(1) = 1. Red squares are the known boundary values; blue dots are the unknowns that the tridiagonal system finds.

blocks.html: The same recipe handles $y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = f(x)$: replace $y'$ by the central difference $\frac{y_{i+1} - y_{i-1}}{2h}$ as well, and the matrix stays tridiagonal. A boundary condition on $y'$ instead of $y$ adds an equation (or a "ghost point") at that end. Very fine grids are cheap thanks to the tridiagonal structure; the limit is round-off, which grows like $1/h^{2}$ as in The Best Step Size.

Treating the known boundary values as unknowns, or leaving them on the left side. $y_0$ and $y_N$ are numbers, not unknowns; the system has $N - 1$ equations in $y_1, \ldots, y_{N-1}$, and $\alpha$ and $\beta$ appear only on the right side of the first and last equations. Check: plug your answer back in, including the boundary values, and every equation should hold.
